evidence.text: The entry gives competing graphic accounts: some oracle-bone forms include 步 interpreted as movement plus phonetic 戉; it also proposes that 歲 was first written by borrowing 戉 and later graphically differentiated. It reports oracle-bone use for ‘year’ and cites a harvest-season explanation, but gives no single settled origin. For small seal script it reports 从步、戌聲. The transmitted Shuowen gloss is Jupiter and describes a twelve-month circuit; CUHK explains the year sense through Jupiter’s cycle. These are source analyses and do not establish a continuous semantic chronology.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 歲

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, transmitted 說文解字 and Duan Yucai commentary
evidence.text: The transmitted entry defines 歲 as Jupiter, describes its passage through the twenty-eight lunar mansions and says it completes a circuit in twelve months. Its graph analysis is 从步戌聲. Duan Yucai explains 步 as regular movement in the sky and also treats 戌 as associative. This is a historical lexicographic analysis, not direct evidence of the earliest graph formation or spoken sense.
evidence.title: 說文解字「歲」— Shuowen.org

evidence.text: The database analyzes 步 as two 止 elements representing alternating feet and gives walking as its basic sense. It cites oracle-bone examples of 步 used for walking. This supports movement as the semantic interpretation in some 歲 analyses, but does not show that every early 歲 form contains 步.

gaps: Oracle-bone ‘year’ and ritual uses remain reports from paleographic sources; primary inscription images and full contexts were not inspected, and the individual artifacts are not absolutely dated here.

The historical path among ritual uses, year/harvest, age, and Jupiter is not demonstrated as a continuous chronology. The Jupiter-to-year explanation is a lexicographic interpretation, not proof of the earliest spoken sense.

For the seal-script component account, Shuowen explicitly labels 戌 as phonetic, but the local Baxter–Sagart readings differ substantially between 戌 (*s.mi[t]) and 歲 (*s-qʷʰat-s). Treat that as a transmitted source analysis, not an independently established historical sound match. The nearby Old Chinese group classification reported by CUHK is not itself a reconstructed pronunciation comparison.

For early 戉, the local Baxter–Sagart values (*[ɢ]ʷat and *s-qʷʰat-s) show a closer comparison, but the weapon’s original spoken name is not independently established. The proposed borrowing may concern the graph rather than a recoverable weapon-name-to-word sound transfer.
The per-character official Unihan pages for 岁, 歲, 步, 戉, and 戌 were inaccessible. Their exact local kMandarin rows were checked but cannot serve as external click-through citations.
